Macworld

Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14, 2026, but development hasn’t stopped. Just two days later on September 16, Apple issued the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, beginning testing of the operating system’s next major point update. Yes, that’s macOS 27.2, not macOS 27.1.

The macOS 27.2 beta gives developers and testers early access to Apple’s latest fixes, refinements and any features that weren’t ready for the initial Golden Gate release.

However, as with any beta software, it may introduce bugs, compatibility problems and poorer battery life so we recommend caution if you wish to install it.

Here’s everything you need to know about the latest macOS beta, including what’s new, when the next public beta is likely to arrive and whether you should install it.

What’s the latest macOS beta?

Apple offers two beta streams: a developer beta and a public beta. The public beta allows enthusiasts and early adopters to test upcoming changes before they are released to everyone. You need to join Apple’s Beta Software Program to access it.

The latest Mac beta is macOS 27.2 beta 4, which Apple released to registered developers on October 13, 2026.

The corresponding macOS 27.2 public beta will be available soon. Public betas usually follow developer betas, although Apple does not guarantee a particular schedule.

macOS 27 Golden Gate beta version tracker

  • Apple released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Developer Beta 4 on October 13, 2026.
  • The macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Public Beta 3 arrived on October 7; new versions are usually released a day or two after the new developer beta.

macOS 26 Tahoe beta: Apple may continue updating macOS 26 Tahoe with security and maintenance releases, but macOS 27 is now the current operating system and the focus of Apple’s beta program.

macOS 27 Beta timeline

What’s new in the latest beta?

Foundry

Apple has not announced any major consumer-facing additions in macOS 27.2 beta 4. The following changes are expected though:

  • Bug fixes and performance improvements: Addressing issues in the first release of macOS 27.
  • Additional Siri AI languages: Apple has said the Siri AI will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in October.
  • Automatic password changes: The promised feature that automatically changes compromised passwords has not yet been implemented, but it could arrive in macOS 27.2..

We’ll update this section as changes are discovered.

See Apple’s developer website for more information about the beta.

Should you install the macOS beta?

Apple

Installing the macOS beta lets you test Apple’s next round of features, fixes and refinements before their public release. Most Mac users should remain on the standard version of macOS 27, particularly if they rely on their Mac for work.

Install if…

  • You need to test apps
  • You want early access to new features
  • You have a secondary Mac available

Wait if…

  • This is your primary work machine
  • You rely on niche or specialist software
  • Stability is critical to your workflow

What are the risks of installing beta software?

Installing pre-release software on a primary device carries several risks.

  • System instability: Performance problems, freezes, crashes, and other unexpected behavior are common during beta testing.
  • App failures: Third-party applications may crash, behave unpredictably, or stop working entirely.
  • Hardware strain: Early beta builds can increase battery drain and cause Macs to run hotter than usual.
  • Data loss: Software bugs may corrupt files, and downgrading to a stable version often requires a complete system reset.

Safety precautions and best practices

If you decide to install the beta, take the following precautions:

  • Use a secondary device: Avoid installing beta software on your primary Mac or on any machine used for critical work.
  • Create a full backup: Use Time Machine to create a complete backup before upgrading so you can restore your Mac if something goes wrong. Note that this needs to be a Time Machine backup from before the beta was installed and you will lose anything saved subsequently.
  • Install on a separate volume: Consider installing the beta on a separate volume or external SSD rather than replacing your main operating system.
  • Check storage space: Make sure you have at least 15GB of free storage available before beginning the installation.

How to install the macOS beta

Foundry

The process for installing a macOS beta depends on whether you are seeking the Developer Beta or the Public Beta. Apple simplified this process a few years ago, removing the need for a paid developer account to access early builds.

The first step is to join Apple’s beta testing program. We explain how to do that in a separate article.

You will need to register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac.

To install the beta follow these steps:

  1. Back up your Mac: Before installing any pre-release software, it is critical to prepare your Mac to avoid data loss. Beta software is inherently unstable and can cause crashes or app compatibility issues.
  2. Register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac:
    For the Public Beta: Visit the Apple Beta Software Program website, sign in with your Apple ID, and agree to the terms.
    For the Developer Beta: Register as an Apple Developer on Apple’s website, download the Apple Developer app from the App Store, sign in with your standard Apple ID, and complete the free registration process.
  3. On the Mac where you wish to install the beta, open System Settings and navigate to General > Software Update.
  4. Click the (i) info button next to Beta Updates.
  5. Enable Beta Updates.
  6. The beta will appear as an available upgrade. Select the macOS beta you want to install (e.g., macOS Public Beta or Developer Beta).
  7. Click Upgrade Now to begin the download and installation.

As long as you are a registered developer or enrolled in the public beta program, when the relevant macOS Beta becomes available, it will also show up on your Mac.

Once you are running the beta, the updates will come through to your Mac automatically; you just need to go to Software Update in System Settings and click to install. See How to install macOS.

How to get a free Apple developer account

If you just want a free Apple Developer account so you can access the beta, you can get this via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app on an iPhone:

  1. Get the Apple Developer App from the App Store. 
  2. Open the app on your iPhone. 
  3. Tap on Account. 
  4. Tap on Sign In. 
  5. Sign in using your usual Apple ID. 

If you wish to actually publish applications to the App Store or receive support, you’ll need to pay $99/£79 per year for a paid account. You can compare the free and paid accounts here.

FAQ

1.

Who can run the macOS beta?

Anyone can run the macOS beta, but to do so, you do need to register for either the developer beta, the public beta, or both.

Apple offers both developer and public beta programs for macOS, enabling all interested users to test pre-release versions of the operating system. While both betas provide early access to new features, they cater to different user profiles based on technical expertise and risk tolerance. Beta software tends to be buggy so the more stable public beta version may be preferable, but even that will not be bug-free.

In the past, the developer beta was only available to developers who had paid to join Apple’s Developer Program (which costs $99/£79). However, for a couple of years now, Apple has opened up the developer beta to registered developers with free developer accounts. We explain how to get a free developer account below.

If you decide you no longer want to run the beta version of macOS read this: How to remove the macOS beta.

2.

macOS public beta vs developer beta

Since 2023, the Developer Beta has been available to anyone who registers as a developer, even if they aren’t a paid-up member of Apple’s Developer Program. As a result, people with a basic free developer account can download the new macOS developer beta (we show you how to register below).

Whether you should download the developer beta if you aren’t a developer is another question. We don’t recommend you install the developer beta if you aren’t a developer. Instead, our recommendation is to use the public beta (the first version of which usually arrives in July).

There are a few differences between the public and developer betas. The public beta is not the same as the beta that is released through the developer program. The public beta typically launches after the developer beta has undergone initial testing and refinement

Developers get updates to their beta first, and possibly more frequently. But you should keep in mind that betas are by nature not stable, and because the public beta comes after the developer beta it could be a little safer to install.

The most significant difference is probably the motive of the testers: Developers usually have the aim of ensuring their apps work when the updated macOS is released to the general public, while public beta testers are essentially helping Apple detect bugs and offering feedback on the features. Because of this, developers may get to test new features not available in the public beta. 

If you want to get the public beta the first thing you need to do, if you haven’t already, is join Apple’s beta programs read this for more information: How to become an Apple beta tester.

3.

Is the macOS beta stable?

By its nature, a beta has the potential to be unstable. Therefore, it’s not advised that you install it on a Mac that you rely on. If you have a second Mac that isn’t mission-critical, then install it there. We strongly recommend that you don’t risk all by putting the macOS beta on your primary Mac, especially not in the early days of the beta development. 

If you don’t have a second Mac, there are a couple of ways you could run macOS beta on your Mac without running the risk of losing data or finding your Mac stops working:

  • We recommend installing it on a partition, which these days is really a volume (and is much easier to create than a partition was). Read about how to do that here: How to dual-boot Mac: Run two versions of macOS on a Mac.
  • Alternatively, you could install the macOS beta on an external drive and run it on that.

We discuss the safety of the macOS beta and the risks you might be taking in more detail in a separate article.

4.

How to prepare your Mac for the beta

At its “Welcome Home” experience, Apple today introduced the all-new HomeView hub, along with the HomePod mini 2 and Apple TV 4K 4. These devices mark Siri AI’s official smart home expansion, bringing its world knowledge and personal context to big screens and smart speakers around the house.

While you may be tempted to rush over to Apple’s website and pre-order a $299 4th-gen Apple TV 4K before the first batch sells out, it may be worth taking a moment to consider if that’s really the right decision. Instead relax, slow down, and read this list of five reasons why I’m not upgrading to the brand-new Apple TV 4K, and why I don’t think you should either.

Common sense

Siri AI publicly launched on iPhones, iPads, Macs, and even Apple Watches with OS 27 last month, and it’s been truly refreshing having a virtual assistant that can actually help. The Apple TV 4K 4 finally adopts this AI-powered foundation, making your smart TVs smarter than ever before. Naturally, most users will want to replace classic Siri with Siri AI in their living rooms, enticing them to buy the 4th-generation Apple TV 4K.

But here’s the thing: Siri AI is not actually exclusive to the Apple TV 4K 4. With the tvOS 27.2 update, the company is also making it available to the 2nd- and 3rd-gen models released in 2021 and 2022.

As long as you’ve paired the device with a compatible iPhone or iPad, you’ll get the same main set of upgraded artificial intelligence tools on your older Apple TV 4K. These include having richer conversations with Siri, executing more complex tasks, tapping into your personal context, and analyzing what’s on your screen.

Foundry

Already listening

To make Siri AI more easily accessible, the Apple TV 4K 4 integrates always-on microphones—sparing you from having to dig out your Siri Remote to trigger the voice assistant. This lets you control the TV in a hands-free manner by uttering the “Siri” or “Hey Siri” hotwords. But what if I told you I’ve already been using Siri on my Apple TV 4K 3 for years without touching its remote?

While the Apple TV 4K 3 and older models don’t independently listen to the wake words, there’s an official workaround that functions reliably. If you depend on a HomePod or HomePod stereo pair for Apple TV 4K audio output, your smart speakers already detect when you summon Siri using your voice and, by default, perform your requests on the paired Apple TV 4K. For example, I yell “Siri, turn on my TV” then “Siri, launch YouTube” all the time, and it correctly opens the app on the big screen—despite the command being processed on the HomePod itself.

Old TV, new remote

Speaking of finding the Siri Remote, the new Apple TV 4K comes with a 4th-gen Siri Remote that introduces proper Find My support. This lets you precisely locate it and have it beep using your iPhone, just like an AirTag. It’s a massive upgrade over the existing location feature, which can’t always pinpoint the lost remote’s whereabouts.

But the good news is that you don’t have to spend $299 to enjoy the benefits of the new Siri Remote.

Apple sells the Siri Remote 4 individually for just $59 (or £59 in the U.K.), and it works with all Apple TV HD and Apple TV 4K models released in 2015 and later. If you often misplace your remote, you can easily remedy the situation by buying a new one separately and pairing it with your current Apple TV box.

Apple

Wasted potential

Perhaps my biggest disappointment lies in the Apple TV 4K 4’s failure to fully leverage its flagship A19 chip. Said processor launched last year with the iPhone 17, making it extraordinarily potent for a media consumption platform like tvOS.

I had hoped Apple would introduce demanding perks that harness the high processing power or announce AAA game partnerships that transform the Apple TV 4K 4 into a mini video game console. Alas, while existing games may run more smoothly on the latest model, the tvOS game library remains exceptionally limited and unappealing to many casual gamers, let alone serious ones. Opting for an A19 set-top box to stream Netflix is objectively wasteful, especially when it costs $299.

Look elsewhere

This brings us to the final argument: what the heck was Apple thinking when it decided to sell the new model for a whopping $299?! For reference, the entry-level Apple TV 4K 3 (64GB, WiFi-only) launched for just $129 in 2022, while the 128GB model with an Ethernet port cost $149 at the time.

While the Apple TV 4K now comes with 128GB of storage and Ethernet support by default, it’s forcing all customers to pay more than twice as much for technology they may not need. Most casual users opt for a Wi-Fi connection, and streaming apps don’t consume a ton of disk space. A Wi-Fi-only configuration would have softened the price hike blow by eliminating unnecessary features that many users won’t touch.

If an upgrade is due, I advise you to buy an Apple TV 4K 3 while you still can (check the price-comparison widget below for any available deals in your area), or look for third-party alternatives such as the $149.99 Google Streamer 4K or Amazon’s even cheaper Fire TV devices. While you won’t get the same Apple ecosystem integrations and personal data sync, they’re arguably not as relevant on a TV. You’ll still be able to download all of your movie streaming apps, including the Apple TV service.

If you depend on a HomePod or HomePod stereo pair for Apple TV 4K audio output, your smart speakers already detect when you summon Siri using your voice and, by default, perform your requests on the paired Apple TV 4K. Apple sells the Siri Remote 4 individually for just $59 (or £59 in the U.K.), and it works with all Apple TV HD and Apple TV 4K models released in 2015 and later. If you often misplace your remote, you can easily remedy the situation by buying a new one separately and pairing it with your current Apple TV box.

Apple

Wasted potential

Perhaps my biggest disappointment lies in the Apple TV 4K 4’s failure to fully leverage its flagship A19 chip. Said processor launched last year with the iPhone 17, making it extraordinarily potent for a media consumption platform like tvOS.

I had hoped Apple would introduce demanding perks that harness the high processing power or announce AAA game partnerships that transform the Apple TV 4K 4 into a mini video game console. Alas, while existing games may run more smoothly on the latest model, the tvOS game library remains exceptionally limited and unappealing to many casual gamers, let alone serious ones. Opting for an A19 set-top box to stream Netflix is objectively wasteful, especially when it costs $299.

While the Apple TV 4K now comes with 128GB of storage and Ethernet support by default, it’s forcing all customers to pay more than twice as much for technology they may not need. Most casual users opt for a Wi-Fi connection, and streaming apps don’t consume a ton of disk space. A Wi-Fi-only configuration would have softened the price hike blow by eliminating unnecessary features that many users won’t touch.

While you won’t get the same Apple ecosystem integrations and personal data sync, they’re arguably not as relevant on a TV. You’ll still be able to download all of your movie streaming apps, including the Apple TV service.

Apple made its big Welcome Home smart home pitch on Tuesday, in which it introduced the new HomeView device, along with upgrades to the Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini. But for anyone worried that there aren’t enough smart home devices that support Apple’s ecosystem (either HomeKit or Matter), there’s also a suite of new smart home gadgets from LG and Schneider Electric.

The Apple Home Collection consists of a set of six items from LG and one item from Schneider Electric. They are not Apple-branded, but have been “designed in collaboration” with Apple and will no doubt be sold in Apple Stores when they become available in December (with some items coming in early 2027).

They appear to be, generally, a little more expensive than comparable smart home items with comparable specs from other brands, but we have yet to see if you can reliably find them on sale at online retailers. Here’s the product list with their retail prices:

LG Video Doorbell: Dual cameras (front and downward to see packages) and a built-in spotlight, with resolution up to 2.5K. $249.95/£229.95 at the Apple Store.

LG Floodlight Cam: Dual motion-activated floodlights and low-light color night vision with camera resolution up to 2.5K. $399.95/£349.95 at the Apple Store.

LG Outdoor Cam: Also offers low-light color vision and 2.5K resolution, but without the floodlights, and with easy self-installation. $299.95/£279.95 at the Apple Store.

LG Indoor Cam: A 2.5K motorized camera that tilts up when you’re away, and points downward when you’re home to protect your privacy. $199.95/£179.95 at the Apple Store.

LG Smart Deadbolt Lock: Using Ultra Wideband, it can detect when a user that has a compatible Home Key on their iPhone is walking up and unlock automatically. You can always tap your iPhone, Apple Watch, use the PIN keypad, or a physical key. $349.95 at the Apple Store (not available in the U.K.).

LG Smart Thermostat: What can you say? It’s a circular smart thermostat that supports the Apple Home thermostat features like Adaptive Temperature. $199.95 at the Apple Store (not available in the U.K.).

Schneider Home Smart Thermostat: The same sort of thing as the LG Smart Thermostat, only with more of a “rounded square” sort of design. $199.95 at the Apple Store (not available in the U.K.).

There are LG and Schneider temperature sensors for other rooms available for $39.95, and some accessories like trim plates and C-wire power adapters.

Of the group, the thermostats seem almost unnecessary. There are a good number of smart home thermostats that support the Matter protocol and therefore work just fine with Apple’s home control and with Siri. Home security cameras that support Apple HomeKit Secure Video are more rare, primarily just from the brands Aqara and Eve. Smart locks that support Apple’s ecosystem are similarly pretty easy to come by with popular brands like Yale, Schlage, Level, and Aqara.

Since the LG cameras use Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video, no extra subscription is required, but the number of cameras supported by HKSV is dependent on your iCloud+ plan. If you have a 50GB plan, it supports a single camera only. The 200GB plan works with up to 5 cameras, and the 2TB plan supports unlimited cameras.

If you want to use Apple Intelligence with these cameras to get smart descriptions and notifications, that’s on a whole other level: you need the 2TB plan to get Apple Intelligence features on a single camera, the 6TB plan for up to 2 cameras, and the 12TB plan to support up to 5 cameras. That’s $59.99 a month in iCloud+ storage subscription fees to get AI summaries on five cameras.

Apple’s newest device isn’t an Apple Watch or an iPhone or even an iPad—but it has elements of all three. Called HomeView, it’s a “personal” smart display designed to be the centerpiece of your home. The screen looks something like a giant Apple Watch, but it’s an entirely new device designed to be touched like an iPad, spun like an iMac G4, and spoken to like a smart speaker, all wrapped up in an adorable package that’s equally at home on a kitchen counter or end table.

You can scroll through the images below to see it in real life, but I wanted to spotlight a couple here too. When mounted on a wall with the wire hidden (no easy task), it looks elegant and futuristic, almost like a visionOS widget. It’s a little thick at nearly 10mm, but the brushed metal case and rounded corners add a sophistication you won’t get with an Echo Show.

Foundry

Of course, most people will opt for the base-attached HomeView, which is actually cheaper than the wall-mounted model when you factor in the cost of a mount and installation. And it’s adorable. It looks something like a mini robot, and I wouldn’t be surprised to see it gain wheels and the ability to automatically swivel when it hears a voice call for Siri. (Honest: Apple is already working on a device that can do that, and this design seems tailor-made for it.)

Foundry

It definitely has personality. There’s a little throwback to the iMac G4 in its design, but it’s also updated to fit today’s aesthetic. The only downside is that it needs to stay near an outlet, so it can’t really exist in the center of a table like Apple is demonstrating in its ads. But I’m kind of in love with its stubby little shape and can’t get enough of its cute footprint. I’ll be buying one.

You can't say squarer than that

It always takes a while to get used to the design of a completely new Apple product. But right now I feel like the HomeView looks weird. And I think it’s because it’s square… or a squircle, technically, because of the rounded corners.

Everyone knows that the squircle was Steve Jobs’ favorite shape, which is why it crops up so much in Apple software design. But it crops up less often in the company’s hardware design, and almost never in the screen. Until now it was just the Apple Watch, which is why Wired described the HomeView as a “giant Apple Watch for the home.”

Screens are expected to be rectangular. That’s why the iPhone Duo looks the way it does. Again, we get used to these things, but at one stage the Duo was called “weird,” “so strange,” and “a little shorty!” It needed to be stubbier than most smartphones so that, when it was unfolded, its screen would be rectangular rather than square.

Apple could very easily have given the HomeView a rectangular screen, so we have to believe the company thinks square is best in this specific use case. You’re not going to be watching movies or TV shows, or playing games. You’re not going to be reading eBooks or lengthy online articles. The screen is just there to let you view your home tech and control it with a few taps, chat to people using FaceTime, and look up the odd recipe. It’s a screen that plays far less of a role than that of an iPhone or a Mac. It really is more like the screen on an Apple Watch.
